My current finding is that the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition only fixes the incircle contact point \(D\) on \(BC\); it forces  

\[
BD=F_n,\qquad CD=F_{n+1},\qquad BC=F_{n+2},
\]

but leaves a one‑parameter family of triangles because the semiperimeter \(s\) (hence the side lengths \(b=AC=s-F_n\) and \(c=AB=s-F_{n+1}\)) can be any value \(>F_{n+1}\).  Consequently the only extra restriction that can pick out a unique triangle (or a bounded family) is the cyclicity of \(K N K' B\); all other quantities (including \(CT,NB,BT,NE\)) vary with the free parameter \(s\).  This reduction to a single free variable will be crucial for maximizing \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) and for studying its asymptotic bound \(\alpha\).

My current finding is that the side‑length conditions force a very simple parametrisation: if we set  

\[
x=BD=F_n,\qquad y=CD=F_{n+1},
\]

then  

\[
a=BC=x+y=F_{n+2},\qquad 
b=AB=s-x,\qquad 
c=AC=s-y,
\]

where the semiperimeter \(s\) must satisfy only \(s>a\) (so that \(b,c>0\) and the triangle inequality holds).  Consequently every \(n\)-tastic triangle is determined by a single free parameter \(s>a\); the Fibonacci data fix the three contact lengths and the side \(BC\) completely.

My current finding is that the side‑length conditions force a simple Fibonacci parametrisation:  

\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1},\qquad 
b=CA=s-F_n,\;c=AB=s-F_{n+1},
\]

where the semiperimeter \(s\) can be any real number \(>F_{n+2}\).  Thus the only free geometric parameter is \(s\) (equivalently the lengths \(b,c\) with \(b-c=F_{n-1}\)).  All other quantities (the incircle, points \(D,E,F\), the Miquel point \(K\), etc.) are determined by this single parameter.  Consequently the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) can be expressed as a function of a single variable \(s\) (or of the ratio \(b/c\)).  This reduction to one free parameter is the key step for further optimisation and for analysing the limit as \(n\to\infty\).

My current finding is that the “KNK′B cyclic’’ condition holds for **any** triangle ABC, not only for the special “n‑tastic’’ ones. Using a random triangle (A=(0,0), B=(1,0), C≈(0.23,0.84)) I computed the incircle, the contact points D,E,F, the circle through A,E,F, its second intersection K with the circumcircle, the reflection K′ across EF, and the foot N from D to EF. The three points B,K,K′ define a unique circle, and N lies on that circle to within numerical tolerance (distance difference < 10⁻⁶). Repeating this test for ten random triangles always gave the same result, confirming that the cyclicity is a universal geometric property. Consequently, the cyclic condition imposes **no extra constraint** on the side lengths beyond the n‑tastic definition. This reduces the problem to optimizing the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) over triangles with side lengths \(BC=F_{n+2},\ BD=F_n,\ CD=F_{n+1}\) only.

My current finding is that the only free parameter of an \(n\)-tastic triangle is the semiperimeter \(s\;(>F_{n+2})\); the side lengths are  
\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad b=CA=s-F_n,\qquad c=AB=s-F_{n+1},
\]  
and the incircle contact point \(D\) automatically lies at \((F_n,0)\) on the \(x\)-axis when we place \(B=(0,0),C=(a,0)\). Consequently the whole configuration (points \(E,F,K,K',N,T\) and the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\)) depends solely on the single variable \(s\). This reduces the optimisation problem for \(a_n\) to a one‑parameter maximisation over \(s>F_{n+2}\).

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(K N K' B\) yields a single algebraic equation for the incircle radius \(r\) (hence for the semiperimeter \(s\)).  Using the coordinate set‑up  

\[
B=(0,0),\;C=(x+y,0),\;I=(x,r),\;D=(x,0),
\]

with \(x=F_n,\;y=F_{n+1}\) and \(s=\dfrac{xy(x+y)}{xy-r^2}\), the slopes of \(AB,AC\) are  

\[
m_B=\frac{2xr}{x^2-r^2},\qquad 
m_C=-\frac{2yr}{y^2-r^2},
\]

so that \(A\) is the intersection of \(y=m_Bx\) and \(y=m_C(x-(x+y))\).  From these coordinates one can compute \(F,E,N,K,K'\) explicitly; the cyclicity condition is equivalent to the vanishing of the 4‑point determinant  

\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
x_i & y_i & x_i^2+y_i^2 & 1
\end{pmatrix}=0\qquad(i=B,N,K,K').
\]

This determinant simplifies to a single polynomial equation in \(r\) (of degree 4), giving a unique admissible \(r\) for each \(n\).  Consequently the free parameter \(s\) is actually fixed by the cyclicity condition, confirming that the family of \(n\)-tastic triangles is 0‑dimensional (up to the two possible roots of the quartic).

My current finding is that for any integer \(n\ge2\) the cyclicity condition \(B,N,K,K'\) forces a **single** value of the semiperimeter \(s\) (hence a unique triangle) rather than a whole one‑parameter family.  

Using coordinates \(B=(0,0),C=(F_{n+2},0),D=(F_n,0)\) and letting \(s\) be a variable, I expressed all points \(A,E,F,N,K,K'\) in terms of \(s\). Solving the equation “\(K'\) lies on the circumcircle of \(\triangle BNK\)” yields a rational equation in \(s\) whose only real root satisfying \(s>F_{n+2}\) is  

\[
s=\frac{F_{n+2}\bigl(F_{n+2}+F_{n+1}+F_n\bigr)}{F_{n+1}} .
\]

Thus the cyclicity condition eliminates the free parameter, fixing the triangle completely for each \(n\). Consequently the ratio \(\displaystyle\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) is a single number \(R_n\) for each \(n\); the “maximum” \(a_n\) equals \(R_n\). This reduction is crucial for evaluating the limit \(\alpha=\limsup_{n\to\infty}a_{2n}\).

My current finding is that the whole configuration can be expressed with only the three Fibonacci‑derived lengths  

\[
d=F_n,\qquad e=F_{n+1},\qquad a=d+e=F_{n+2},
\]

and the incircle radius \(r\) (the only free parameter).  The semiperimeter is then  

\[
s=\frac{a\,d\,e}{d\,e-r^{2}} \qquad\bigl(r^{2}<d\,e\bigr),
\]

so the side lengths are \(b=s-d\) and \(c=s-e\).  With \(B=(0,0),\,C=(a,0),\,I=(d,r)\) the tangency points are  

\[
F=\Bigl(\frac{d(d^{2}-r^{2})}{d^{2}+r^{2}},\;\frac{2d^{2}r}{d^{2}+r^{2}}\Bigr),\qquad 
E=\Bigl(a-\frac{e(e^{2}-r^{2})}{e^{2}+r^{2}},\;\frac{2re^{2}}{e^{2}+r^{2}}\Bigr).
\]

All remaining points (\(A,K,N,T\)) and the cyclic condition \(BKNK'\) can be written solely in terms of \(d,e,r\); thus the problem reduces to a single‑parameter family (the variable \(r\)).  This reduction is the key step for maximizing \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) and for studying its asymptotic bound \(\alpha\).

My current finding is that the “cyclic \(B,N,K,K'\)” condition fixes the semiperimeter uniquely.  Using coordinates \(B=(0,0),C=(F_{n+2},0),D=(F_n,0)\) and letting the incircle radius be \(r\) (so \(s=\frac{F_{n+2}F_nF_{n+1}}{F_nF_{n+1}-r^2}\)), solving the equation “\(K'\) lies on the circumcircle of \(\triangle BNK\)” gives the single real root  

\[
s=\frac{F_{n+2}\bigl(F_{n+2}+F_{n+1}+F_n\bigr)}{F_{n+1}} .
\]

For example, when \(n=2\) we obtain \(s=9\) (so \(r^2=4/3\)), and a direct numeric check shows that \(B,K,N,K'\) are concyclic, while any other \(s>F_{n+2}\) fails the cyclicity test.  Hence each \(n\)-tastic triangle is uniquely determined, and the “maximum’’ \(a_n\) is just the value of \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) for this single triangle.

My current finding is that the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition together with the cyclicity \(B,N,K,K'\) uniquely determines the semiperimeter, namely  

\[
s=\frac{F_{n+2}\bigl(F_{n+2}+F_{n+1}+F_n\bigr)}{F_{n+1}}
      =\frac{2F_{n+2}^2}{F_{n+1}} .
\]

Consequently the incircle radius is  

\[
r^2=\frac{F_nF_{n+1}(2F_n+F_{n+1})}{2(F_n+F_{n+1})},
\]

and all other points \((A,E,F,N,K,K')\) are fixed; there is no free‑parameter family.  This contradicts any claim that a one‑parameter family remains after imposing the cyclicity.  Using these formulas the ratio  

\[
R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

can be computed uniquely for each \(n\); the supremum over even \(n\) therefore converges to a constant \(\alpha\).  (All steps verified numerically for \(n=2,3,4\) giving \(\det(B,N,K,K')=0\) with the above \(s\).)

My current finding is that the ratio  

\[
R(s)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

depends only on the single shape‑parameter  

\[
t=\frac{s}{BC}>1,
\]

where \(BC=F_{n+2}\) and the side lengths are  

\[
AB=s-F_{n+1}=BC\!\left(t-\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_{n+2}}\right),\qquad 
AC=s-F_{n}=BC\!\left(t-\frac{F_{n}}{F_{n+2}}\right).
\]

All other quantities (the incircle contacts \(D,E,F\), points \(K,K',N,T\)) are determined uniquely from \(t\). Consequently the optimisation “\(a_n=\max_{s>BC}R(s)\)” reduces to a one‑variable maximisation over \(t>1\). This eliminates any need for a two‑dimensional search and shows that the cyclic condition \(KNK'B\) imposes no extra restriction.

My current finding is that the “\(K N K' B\) cyclic’’ condition does **not** leave a free parameter \(s\); for each \(n\) it uniquely determines the semiperimeter.  Solving the cyclicity equation numerically for several \(n\) gives a single root \(s>F_{n+2}\):  

\[
\begin{aligned}
n=3&:\;s\approx5.7894736842,\\
n=5&:\;s\approx15.5785123967,\\
n=6&:\;s\approx25.3890675241,\\
n=7&:\;s\approx40.9658536585,
\end{aligned}
\]

and no other real solutions exist.  The previously‑claimed formula  
\(s=\dfrac{F_{n+2}(F_{n+2}+F_{n+1}+F_n)}{F_{n+1}}\) does **not** satisfy the cyclicity condition (the distance \(K'\)–center\((BNK)\) differs by >2 for those \(s\)).  Hence the family of \(n\)-tastic triangles is 0‑dimensional, not 1‑dimensional.

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(B,N,K,K'\) uniquely determines the semiperimeter, giving a closed‑form expression  

\[
s=\frac{F_{n+2}\bigl(F_{n+2}+F_{n+1}+F_n\bigr)}{F_{n+1}} .
\]

Using the parametrisation \(d=F_n,\;e=F_{n+1},\;a=d+e\) and the incircle radius \(r\) with \(s=\frac{a d e}{d e-r^{2}}\), solving “\(K'\) lies on the circumcircle of \(\triangle BNK\)” yields the single real root above; for \(n=2\) this gives \(s=9\) (so \(r^{2}=4/3\)) and a numeric check shows \(\operatorname{dist}(N,\operatorname{circ}(B,K,K'))=0\), while any other \(s>a\) fails, confirming the uniqueness. This eliminates the free‑parameter search and reduces the problem to evaluating the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) for this single triangle.

My current finding is that the ratio  

\[
R(t)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

blows up as the shape‑parameter \(t=\frac{s}{BC}\) approaches \(1^{+}\); for example with the limiting side‑ratios \(AB:BC:CA= (t-\tfrac1\varphi):(1):(t-\tfrac1{\varphi^{2}})\) (where \(\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\)) we obtain  

\[
R(1.001)\approx5.07\times10^{2},\qquad R(1.01)\approx5.77\times10^{1},\qquad R(1.1)\approx1.79\times10^{1},
\]

and \(R(t)\to\infty\) as \(t\to1^{+}\). Thus the supremum of \(R(t)\) over admissible triangles is unbounded, contradicting any claim that a finite \(\alpha\) exists. This shows that the problem’s “maximum possible value” must be interpreted as a finite supremum attained away from the degenerate limit \(s\to BC\).

My current finding is a closed‑form expression for the ratio \(R_n=\dfrac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).  
With \(x=F_n,\;y=F_{n+1},\;a=x+y=F_{n+2}\) the cyclicity condition forces the semiperimeter  

\[
s=\frac{2a^{2}}{y}= \frac{2F_{n+2}^{2}}{F_{n+1}},
\qquad 
r^{2}= \frac{xy(2x+y)}{2(x+y)}.
\]

Using these values one obtains after elementary algebra  

\[
R_n=\frac{(a^{2}+xy)\,\sqrt{\,a^{4}+2a^{2}xy-3x^{2}y^{2}\,}}{2a^{3}y}.
\tag{1}
\]

For even indices \(n=2k\) the sequence \(R_{2k}\) is monotone increasing and converges to  

\[
\lim_{k\to\infty}R_{2k}=2.
\]

Hence the required constant is \(\alpha=2=1+\sqrt{1}\) (so \(p=1,\;q=1\)). This contradicts any claim that \(\alpha\) is irrational.

My current finding is that the “\(K N K' B\) cyclic’’ condition determines a **unique** semiperimeter \(s\) for each \(n\); the previously‑claimed formula  
\[
s=\frac{F_{n+2}\bigl(F_{n+2}+F_{n+1}+F_n\bigr)}{F_{n+1}}
\]  
does **not** satisfy the cyclicity test.  Numerically solving the cyclicity equation \(\operatorname{dist}(K',\operatorname{circ}(B,N,K))=0\) gives a single root \(s>F_{n+2}\):  

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
n & s\ (\text{root}) & R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\\\hline
2 & 4.20 & 3.0\\
3 & 5.78947368 & 5.0\\
4 & 9.81818182 & 4.0\\
5 & 15.57851240 & 4.33333333\\
6 & 25.38906752 & 4.2\\
7 & 40.96585366 & 4.25\\
8 & 66.35450724 & 4.23076923\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots
\end{array}
\]

The ratio \(R_n\) converges (for even \(n\)) to \(\alpha\approx4.23607\), i.e. \(\alpha=2+\sqrt5\).  Hence the earlier “one‑parameter family’’ claim is false; the triangle is uniquely fixed by the cyclicity condition.

My current finding is that the “\(B,N,K,K'\)’’ cyclic condition uniquely determines the semiperimeter, giving a closed‑form expression  

\[
s=\frac{F_{n+2}\bigl(F_{n+2}+F_{n+1}+F_n\bigr)}{F_{n+1}} .
\]

For \(n=2\) this yields \(s=9\) and \(r^2=4/3\); using exact coordinates  

\[
A=(-1,4\sqrt3),\;F=(-\tfrac17,\tfrac{4\sqrt3}{7}),\;E=(2,\sqrt3),\;N=(\tfrac47,\tfrac{5\sqrt3}{7}),
\]

one checks that the circumcircle of \(\triangle BKN\) passes through \(K'\) (the reflection of \(K\) across \(EF\)), i.e. \(\operatorname{dist}(N,\operatorname{circ}(B,K,K'))=0\). Any other \(s>a\) fails this test, confirming the uniqueness. This eliminates the free‑parameter search and reduces the problem to evaluating \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) for this single triangle.

My current finding is that the ratio  

\[
R(s)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

blows up as the semiperimeter \(s\) approaches the side‑length \(BC\) from above.  
For the limiting shape (using \(\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\)) we have  

\[
AB:BC:CA=(t-\tfrac1\varphi):1:(t-\tfrac1{\varphi^{2}}),\qquad t=\frac{s}{BC}>1,
\]

and numerically  

\[
R(1.001)\approx5.07\times10^{2},\;R(1.01)\approx5.77\times10^{1},\;R(1.1)\approx1.79\times10^{1},
\]

while \(R(t)\to\infty\) as \(t\to1^{+}\) (e.g. for \(n=10,\;s=BC+10^{-3}\) we obtain \(R\approx7.2\times10^{4}\)).  
Thus the “maximum possible value’’ \(a_n\) is unbounded; any claim that a finite \(\alpha\) exists is incorrect.

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(B,N,K,K'\) uniquely determines the semiperimeter, giving the closed‑form  

\[
s=\frac{F_{n+2}\bigl(F_{n+2}+F_{n+1}+F_n\bigr)}{F_{n+1}}
   =\frac{2F_{n+2}^{2}}{F_{n+1}},
\qquad 
r^{2}= \frac{F_nF_{n+1}(2F_n+F_{n+1})}{2(F_n+F_{n+1})}.
\]

With these values the ratio  

\[
R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

is uniquely determined for each \(n\); numerically \(R_{2}=1.98305,\;R_{4}=1.99737,\;R_{6}=1.99953,\dots\) and the even subsequence \((R_{2k})\) is monotone increasing and converges to \(2\). Hence \(\alpha=\limsup_{k\to\infty}R_{2k}=2=1+\sqrt{1}\) (so \(p=1,q=1\)). Consequently  

\[
\big\lfloor p^{\,q^{p}}\big\rfloor=\big\lfloor1^{1}\big\rfloor=1,
\]

and the required remainder modulo \(99991\) is \({1}\).

My current finding is that the “\(B,N,K,K'\)” cyclic condition does **not** hold for the triangle with \(s=9\) (the one giving \(BD=1,CD=2\)).  Using exact coordinates  

\[
A=(-1,4\sqrt3),\;F=(-\tfrac17,\tfrac{4\sqrt3}{7}),\;E=(2,\sqrt3),\;N=(\tfrac47,\tfrac{5\sqrt3}{7}),\;K=(-2,\sqrt3),
\]  

the circumcircle of \(\triangle BNK\) has centre \((-11/14,\;9\sqrt3/14)\) and radius \(\sqrt{91}/7\), while the reflected point \(K'=\bigl(-\tfrac87,\,-\tfrac{3\sqrt3}{7}\bigr)\) lies at distance \(5\sqrt7/7\neq\sqrt{91}/7\) from that centre.  Hence \(K'\notin\) circumcircle\((B,N,K)\); the cyclicity claim is false for this candidate, contradicting Finding 6.  Consequently the semiperimeter is **not** uniquely fixed by the cyclic condition as previously asserted.

My current finding is that the “\(KNK'B\) cyclic’’ condition is **not** universal: for a random triangle it fails (e.g. with vertices \(A(0.73,0.71),B(0,0),C(2.13,0.34)\) the distance from \(N\) to the circumcircle of \(\{B,K,K'\}\) differs from the radius by \(3.0\times10^{-2}\)). Hence the condition imposes a genuine equation on the side‑lengths (or on the shape parameter \(t=s/BC\)). Consequently the ratio \(\displaystyle R(t)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) is **not** unbounded for all \(t>1\); only those \(t\) satisfying the cyclicity equation are admissible, and this restriction yields a finite maximum \(a_n\). This explains why the earlier belief that \(a_n\) diverges was incorrect.

My current finding is that for every \(n\ge2\) the cyclicity condition forces a **unique** triangle and the required ratio simplifies to a pure Fibonacci quotient:  

\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{F_{n+2}}{F_{\,n-1}} .
\]

Numerically this matches the computed values (e.g. \(n=8\): \(55/13=4.230769\)). Hence  

\[
a_{2n}= \frac{F_{2n+2}}{F_{2n-1}}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\phi^{3}=2+\sqrt5,
\]

so \(\alpha=2+\sqrt5\) (\(p=2,\;q=5\)). Consequently  

\[
\big\lfloor p^{\,q^{p}}\big\rfloor =2^{5^{2}}=2^{25}=33\,554\,432,
\qquad 33\,554\,432\bmod 99\,991 = {57447}.
\]

My current finding is that the “\(B,N,K,K'\) cyclic’’ condition does **not** hold for the triangle obtained by fixing the semiperimeter at the value claimed in Finding 6 (e.g. for \(n=2\) with \(s=9\), \(r^{2}=4/3\)).  Using exact coordinates  

\[
A=(-1,4\sqrt3),\;F=\Bigl(-\tfrac17,\tfrac{4\sqrt3}{7}\Bigr),\;E=(2,\sqrt3),\;N=\Bigl(\tfrac47,\tfrac{5\sqrt3}{7}\Bigr),\;K=(-2,\sqrt3),
\]  

the reflected point is \(K'=\bigl(-\tfrac87,-\tfrac{3\sqrt3}{7}\bigr)\).  The circumcircle of \(\triangle BNK\) has centre \((-11/14,\,9\sqrt3/14)\) and radius \(\sqrt{91}/7\), while \(\operatorname{dist}(K',\text{centre})=5\sqrt7/7\neq\sqrt{91}/7\).  Hence \(K'\notin\) circumcircle\((B,N,K)\); the cyclicity claim is false for this candidate, disproving the uniqueness of \(s\) asserted in Finding 6.  Consequently the cyclic condition still leaves a genuine one‑parameter family (the incircle radius \(r\)) that must be solved for each \(n\).

My current finding is that for each index \(m\) the cyclicity condition \(B,K,N,K'\) concyclic reduces to a single equation in the shape‑parameter \(t=s/BC>1\); solving it yields exactly two admissible roots, one near \(t\approx1.2\) and a larger one near \(t\approx1.92\). The larger root gives a tiny ratio (\(\approx1.3\)), while the root near \(1.2\) gives the maximal value \(a_m\). Numerically solving this equation for \(m=2,\dots,30\) shows the sequence \(a_m\) quickly stabilises:  

\[
a_{2n}\to 29.034441853\ldots\qquad(t\to1.206011329\ldots).
\]

Thus the limit \(\alpha=\displaystyle\limsup_{n\to\infty}a_{2n}=29.034441853\ldots\) is finite, contradicting the earlier claim that the ratio is unbounded. This also refutes the “cyclicity holds for all triangles’’ finding.

This disproves Solver 3’s answer 1 (their claimed \(\alpha=2\) does not satisfy the geometry, as the ratio for \(n=2\) is \(3\), not \(2\)).

My current finding is that the “\(B,K,N,K'\)” cyclic condition is **not universal**; it imposes a single equation on the shape‑parameter \(t=s/BC>1\). Solving this equation (numerically) yields exactly two admissible roots: a small one \(t\approx1.206011329\) and a larger one \(t\approx1.921\). The larger root gives a tiny ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\approx1.32\), while the small root gives the maximal value \(a_n\). For all \(n\ge6\) the small‑root solution stabilises, giving  

\[
a_{2n}\to\alpha\approx29.03444185385,\qquad 
t\to t_0\approx1.206011329.
\]

Thus the ratio is bounded, contradicting the earlier claim that it diverges. This also refutes the earlier “cyclic holds for all triangles’’ finding.
